assessment:
In this study, Homan and colleagues investigate the role of complement receptor C3aR1 in macrophages and Kupffer cells in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The authors were motivated by previous findings showing that whole-body C3aR1 deletion protects mice from diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis, yet the specific contribution of macrophage C3aR1 signaling remained unclear. Using cell-type-specific knockout approaches, they generated mice lacking C3aR1 in all macrophages (C3aR1-MφKO) or specifically in liver-resident Kupffer cells (C3aR1-KpKO) and subjected them to the GAN diet, a well-validated dietary model that recapitulates key features of human MASLD/MASH.

The key findings demonstrate that neither macrophage-specific nor Kupffer cell-specific deletion of C3aR1 affects body weight gain, glucose homeostasis, hepatic steatosis, inflammation, or fibrosis in the GAN diet model. The authors first establish that macrophages account for approximately 88% of hepatic C3ar1 expression, with Kupffer cells contributing about 80%, confirming these cell types as the predominant source of C3aR1 in the liver. Despite achieving near-complete ablation of hepatic C3ar1 expression in both knockout models, comprehensive metabolic phenotyping revealed no significant differences in weight gain, body composition, glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, liver mass, or histological markers of steatosis and fibrosis compared to controls. Gene expression analysis similarly showed no changes in markers of inflammation, fibrosis, or lipid metabolism. These findings contrast sharply with previous reports of whole-body C3aR1 knockout mice, suggesting that the metabolic protection observed in those studies is mediated by C3aR1 signaling in non-macrophage cell types.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is solid and comprehensive. The authors employ appropriate genetic models with validated deletion of C3ar1 in target cell populations, use a well-characterized dietary model of MASLD/MASH, and provide multiple complementary measures of metabolic and hepatic phenotypes including body composition, glucose homeostasis tests, histological quantification, and gene expression analysis. The consistency of null findings across both knockout models and multiple outcome measures strengthens confidence in the conclusions. However, some limitations warrant consideration. The authors acknowledge that relatively low levels of fibrosis were observed in their study, potentially due to initiating the diet at a young age, which may have limited their ability to detect effects on advanced fibrosis. Additionally, while the GAN diet model recapitulates many features of human MASLD/MASH, testing in alternative models of liver injury might reveal context-dependent roles for macrophage C3aR1. The study also does not address potential compensatory mechanisms, such as upregulation of the related receptor C5aR1, which could mask effects of C3aR1 deletion.

This work makes a valuable contribution to understanding the cell-type-specific roles of complement signaling in metabolic liver disease. By demonstrating that macrophage and Kupffer cell C3aR1 is dispensable for MASLD pathogenesis in this model, the study helps refine our understanding of which cellular compartments mediate complement effects on metabolism. The findings have important implications for therapeutic targeting of the complement system in MASLD, suggesting that strategies focused solely on macrophage C3aR1 may be insufficient. The careful characterization of C3aR1 expression patterns across liver cell types and the rigorous negative results provide important foundational knowledge for the field, even as they raise new questions about which cell types mediate the metabolic effects of whole-body C3aR1 deletion.
